cards.front: Fetch rate for 15B pages in 4 weeks
cards.back: 4 weeks is about 2.4M seconds, so about 6,200 pages a second. Plan for 2× to absorb slow hosts and retries.
About 1.5 PB at 100 KB a page, 2.14 PB provisioned at 70% full. HTML compresses 5-10×.

cards.front: Size of a URL-seen checksum set
cards.back: 15B × 8 bytes = 120 GB, the same again for content checksums. Fine when sharded.
An in-memory buffer up to ~64 KB, spilling to a temp file, so several processors read the same page without refetching it.
Front queues order URLs by priority; each back queue holds one host, and a heap orders hosts by the earliest time each may be contacted again.

cards.front: How the next allowed time for a host is set
cards.back: Now plus a delay, such as 10× the last response time or the robots.txt crawl delay.
About a day per host, so it isn't fetched before every page.

cards.front: Why run a local caching DNS resolver?
cards.back: 6,200 fetches a second would mean thousands of lookups a second, often through synchronous libraries. DNS is the classic hidden bottleneck.
URL-seen runs before adding to the frontier on a normalized URL hash; content-seen runs after fetching on a checksum, catching mirrors and session IDs.

cards.front: The Bloom filter's flaw for a crawler
cards.back: A false positive treats a new URL as seen, so it is never crawled. About 10 bits per item gives about 1% false positives.

cards.front: The strongest signal of a crawler trap
cards.back: An impossibly large number of URLs for one host compared with its importance. Per-host budgets scaled by importance bound every trap.
Consistent hashing of the hostname picks the node owning that host's queue, seen-set shards and caches, so politeness needs no coordination.

quiz.q: A site owner complains the crawler is opening dozens of connections at once to their server. Which design piece should prevent this?
choices: Per-host back queues mapped to a single worker, with a next-allowed-time heap
quiz.why: One host maps to one back queue and one worker, with a delay between requests.

quiz.q: Fetch throughput is well below target even though fetchers have idle CPU. Which component is most likely the bottleneck?
quiz.why: Thousands of synchronous lookups a second stall fetchers unless DNS is cached and asynchronous.

quiz.q: A low-importance site appears in the top 100 hosts by URL count in the frontier, with URLs like /calendar?date=2391-04-17. What is the defence?
choices: Fetch it faster to finish sooner
Per-host page budgets scaled by importance, plus URL pattern detection
quiz.why: Budgets turn every trap into a bounded cost.

quiz.q: Important new pages are mysteriously never crawled. The URL-seen set is a small Bloom filter. Why?
choices: False positives mark them as already seen
quiz.why: Size the filter generously or confirm positives against the exact store for important URLs.

quiz.q: A crawler node dies in week three. How does the crawl continue without starting over?
choices: Neighbours take its hosts via consistent hashing and load its latest checkpoint
A standby replays all fetches from Kafka
quiz.why: Frequent checkpoints mean a failure costs minutes; dedupe makes redone work harmless.

quiz.q: The same article is stored thousands of times under URLs that differ only by ?sid=... What catches it?
choices: Normalizing session parameters, with the content-seen test catching the rest
quiz.why: Session IDs are stripped in normalization and duplicates caught by content checksum.

quiz.q: Recrawling a news site, most pages haven't changed. How do you save bandwidth?
choices: Use If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match so unchanged pages return 304
quiz.why: Conditional requests cost a 304 with no body for unchanged pages.
